source.title: Stop Probing, Start Coding: Why Linear Probes and Sparse Autoencoders Fail at Compositional Generalisation
source.authors: Vit'oria Barin-Pacela; S. Joshi; I. Camacho; Simon Lacoste-Julien; D. Klindt

record.file_problem: Whole paper text, including appendices, is present. The Pythia results table has a caption that identifies Gemma-2-2B, although the surrounding text identifies the results as Pythia-70M-deduped; this inconsistency is noted on the affected rows.
record.tranche_reason: Tests task-level usefulness of sparse codes on real LLM activations, a new setting relevant as indirect evidence for V4. It does not directly establish feature recovery or the geometry claimed in V1.
record.gate_note: The real-LLM experiments report sparse-probing test accuracy by method and dataset; those are recorded below as indirect task-level evidence for V4. The paper also reports synthetic recovery, phase-transition, and dictionary-quality experiments, but they do not measure the feature-direction geometry, polysemanticity, or one-dimensional-versus-multidimensional feature structure named by the other versions. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the superposition (linear compressed-sensing) framework and compares inference methods within it: DL-FISTA, SAEs and linear probes. Its synthetic data come from a random Gaussian mixing matrix, not a trained network, so they cannot show how networks store features (V1). The real-LLM results are sparse-probing accuracies of different codes. These measure the study's method against SAEs and probes, not whether LLMs spread features across neurons or contain recoverable sparse features (V4). No version is tested directly. The relevant findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The central conclusion is that SAE failure under compositional OOD shift in synthetic superposition is a dictionary-learning problem, not an inference problem. An oracle dictionary shows the task is solvable, and scalable dictionary learning is the key open problem. On real LLMs, per-sample sparse coding is feasible at d_h up to 16,384. DL-FISTA slightly exceeds raw probing on Pythia (92.38 vs 92.21) and on six of eight Gemma datasets, and beats Top-K SAEs on all eight. SAE codes never exceed raw probing. The authors note real-data results are in-distribution only.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random sparse latent projections and compares sparse coding, SAE encoders, and downstream probes; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-geometry experiments. Its real-LLM evaluation is sparse probing on classification datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Model and layer (Pythia-70M-deduped layer 4; Gemma-2-2B layer 12) and dataset; the Gemma method ordering varies by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic linear mixtures with known dictionaries, SAE decoder columns point in wrong directions (cosine 0.33–0.93) and SAE MCC plateaus at 0.2–0.5. Per-sample FISTA with the oracle dictionary reaches MCC ≥0.95. Swapping in FISTA on the SAE dictionary does not close the gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs fail to recover ground-truth sparse latents and dictionaries in synthetic superposition data, with dictionary learning as the bottleneck. Bears on, but does not test, V5 in real models.

fits_no_version.finding: In an undersampling sweep, per-sample recovery shows a compressed-sensing phase transition near δ ≥ 2ρ ln(1/ρ). SAEs plateau below it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recoverability of superposed sparse codes follows compressed-sensing bounds for per-sample inference but not for amortised SAEs. This is recovery, not network representation geometry (V1).

fits_no_version.finding: On real LLM activations, SAE code probing accuracy matches raw activations on Pythia and trails it on all eight Gemma-2-2B datasets. DL-FISTA codes exceed SAE codes on all eight and raw activations on six.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream sparse-probing usefulness of SAE versus per-sample sparse codes on LLM activations.

record.problems: Real-LLM experiments have no ground-truth feature labels and do not use compositional OOD splits, as the authors acknowledge. They test only two models/layers. The Pythia table caption conflicts with the surrounding text about the model identity; the text also describes uncertainty differently from the Table 3 caption.
record.rows_left_out: No real-LLM rows were left out. Synthetic MCC, accuracy, cosine, and support-recovery results were not entered as rows because they do not directly measure the specific feature geometry, polysemanticity, or dimensionality claims in the listed versions.

untested.parts: No trained toy network. Synthetic data use a fixed random Gaussian mixing, so there is no learned feature geometry or sparsity-dependent storage transition. The phase transition reported is compressed-sensing recovery, not representation.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity allocation are not measured.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
No measure of features spread across neurons or of sparse-feature recovery in real LLMs. Only probing accuracy of codes is reported.
No test of stability, completeness or canonicity of SAE features in real models. Dictionary non-recovery is shown only on synthetic linear mixtures.
1-D features are assumed by definition; multi-dimensional features are not compared.

record.verdict_notes: Changed from tests/T3 to assumes/T4. The paper builds on the superposition framing to compare sparse-inference methods. Its synthetic data are random linear mixtures, not trained networks, and its LLM results are probing accuracies. All reader labels removed. Table 3's caption is mis-copied from Table 2: it says Gemma and 'six of eight' while the prose says Pythia. The Gemma 'instruct' stage is not stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether trained toy networks store features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, or whether their feature geometry is regular. Its synthetic compressed-sensing recovery and sparsity/undersampling sweeps do not test that representation-geometry claim.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.

Tests downstream task accuracy from SAE and learned sparse codes on real-model activations as indirect evidence only. It does not establish that features are spread across neurons, directly recover ground-truth features, or test compositional OOD generalisation on real text.
Discusses identifiability concerns, but does not test whether SAE features are stable across runs or constitute complete, canonical units in real models.
Treats code coordinates as one-dimensional features in its setup but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Sparse-probing logistic classifier on raw activations

conditions.value: eight text-classification datasets; aggregate as reported

rows.uncertainty: ± 0.16; text identifies standard deviation over three seeds
rows.note: The table caption calls this Gemma-2-2B, but the surrounding prose and setup identify the result as Pythia-70M-deduped. The paper reports this as the raw-activation reference.
rows.check: Raw-activation probe accuracy is a comparator for the method comparison, not a measure of feature superposition or recovery in Pythia. Table 3's caption wrongly names Gemma-2-2B and claims six of eight datasets; Section 4.4 prose and D.3 identify Pythia-70M-deduped layer 4.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Sparse-probing logistic classifier on SAE codes

conditions.value: eight text-classification datasets; aggregate as reported

rows.uncertainty: ± 0.02; table caption says standard deviation over three seeds
rows.note: SAE codes match the raw-activation probe on this aggregate task score; this is indirect evidence of task-relevant information, not direct feature recovery. The table caption has the model-name inconsistency noted above.
rows.check: SAE code probing accuracy (92.21, the same as raw) shows task information is retained. It does not show that sparse features exist or are recovered, so it cannot be scored against V4. The caption has the same model-name error.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Sparse-probing logistic classifier on DL-FISTA codes

conditions.value: eight text-classification datasets; aggregate as reported

rows.uncertainty: ± 0.07; text identifies standard deviation over three seeds
rows.note: The authors call this a small, seed-consistent margin. The method is DL-FISTA, not an SAE. The table caption has the model-name inconsistency noted above.
rows.check: This is the study's own method (DL-FISTA) compared with others, not a measure of the phenomenon. The 92.38 vs 92.21 margin is a method-performance result.
